name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
overview: This is the other major front door, alongside T1566's phishing coverage already in this tool: rather than tricking a human into clicking something, the adversary exploits a bug, misconfiguration, or unpatched CVE directly in whatever internet-facing software the organization runs — a web application, a VPN gateway, an email server, a database, a network device's management interface. It is, without exaggeration, one of the defining initial-access stories of the last several years: Log4j, ProxyLogon/ProxyShell against Exchange, and a long parade of edge-device CVEs (Citrix ADC, Pulse Secure, FortiGate, Ivanti) have each individually produced mass-exploitation events, and nearly every major APT and ransomware group referenced anywhere in this tool shows up in this pack's procedure examples specifically because a patchable vulnerability sitting on the internet is a lower-effort, higher-success-rate entry point than convincing a human to do anything at all.

prerequisite_concepts.term: This is the initial-access technique where patching IS the primary detection strategy
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: Nearly every named CVE in this pack's procedure examples was patchable well before it was mass-exploited — CVE-2019-19781 (Citrix), CVE-2021-44228 (Log4j), CVE-2021-26855 (ProxyLogon) all had vendor fixes available, frequently for weeks or months, before opportunistic and targeted exploitation caught up. That makes vulnerability and patch management the single highest-leverage control in this entire pack, more than almost any other technique in TTPHUNT — a hunt program here is explicitly a backstop for a patching program, not a replacement for one.

prerequisite_concepts.term: The attack chain has a repeatable four-stage shape regardless of which specific CVE is used
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: An abnormal HTTP/S request or unusual method hits the application, the application responds with an elevated error code or a WAF block, the underlying service process spawns a shell or LOLBin it never should, and that shell reaches out for C2 — this same shape repeats whether the exploited application is IIS, Exchange, a Kubernetes ingress, or a network device's management interface. Detection strategies across the sub-surfaces in this technique all correlate the same three-step pattern (anomalous request, service-process-spawns-shell, outbound callback) rather than needing a unique detection built for every individual CVE.

prerequisite_concepts.term: A shell spawned by a service process is almost always the actual tell, not the initial request
prerequisite_concepts.explanation: The exploit request itself frequently looks like ordinary, if unusual, web traffic and is easy to miss in isolation — but IIS's w3wp.exe, Apache/nginx's worker process, or vCenter's hostd/vpxd process spawning cmd.exe, bash, or PowerShell is something that essentially never happens as part of that service's normal function. That single behavioral fact (a web-facing service process becoming a shell's parent) is the highest-confidence, most durable detection signal in this entire pack, and it holds up regardless of whether the specific CVE involved is one a hunter has ever heard of.

subtechniques.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application
subtechniques.overview: Adversaries target software bugs, misconfigurations, or unpatched CVEs in anything internet-facing — web servers (IIS, Apache, Nginx), databases, VPN/gateway appliances (Citrix ADC, Pulse Secure, FortiGate), email servers (Microsoft Exchange, Zimbra), collaboration platforms (SharePoint, Confluence), virtualization infrastructure (VMware vCenter), and network device management protocols (SNMP, Cisco Smart Install) — to gain initial network access with no social engineering required at all. The procedure examples here read like a timeline of the industry's biggest incidents: APT29's exploitation of Citrix, Pulse Secure, and FortiGate CVEs; HAFNIUM's Exchange zero-days; Volt Typhoon's and Salt Typhoon's edge-device campaigns against critical infrastructure; and Magic Hound's and countless ransomware operators' rapid weaponization of Log4j within days of disclosure.

concepts.term: Edge devices are now a preferred target precisely because they can't run traditional EDR
concepts.explanation: VPN gateways, firewalls, and similar appliances run closed, vendor-controlled operating systems that a defender cannot install an EDR agent onto, which means an adversary who compromises one of these devices operates in a genuine visibility blind spot no amount of endpoint tooling elsewhere in the environment can see into. Volt Typhoon's and Salt Typhoon's well-documented targeting of exactly this device category reflects a deliberate strategic choice, not coincidence — these are consistently the quietest possible place to sit inside a network specifically because normal host-based detection has no presence there at all.

concepts.term: Container and cloud variants extend this technique past the traditional web server
concepts.explanation: In a containerized or cloud-hosted environment, the same exploitation pattern can lead not just to a shell on a single host but to direct access to the cloud metadata service (169.254.169.254) — which frequently hands over the temporary credentials the workload itself uses, turning one exploited application into a path toward the surrounding cloud account's IAM permissions. A Kubernetes-specific variant of the same idea shows up as kubectl exec or a sidecar spawning immediately following an ingress anomaly, which is why this pack's detection queries explicitly include a metadata-service-access check alongside the more traditional shell-spawn pattern.

concepts.term: Time-to-exploitation has compressed from months to days, and detection timelines have to match
concepts.explanation: Log4j and several of the edge-device CVEs referenced in this pack's procedure examples saw mass opportunistic scanning and exploitation within days of public disclosure — sometimes before a patch was even available, based on proof-of-concept code circulating publicly. That compression means the traditional 30/60/90-day patch cycle many vulnerability management programs are built around is now frequently too slow on its own for internet-facing systems specifically, which is exactly why this pack's mitigation list leads with rapid response to critical disclosures rather than routine patch cadence alone.

procedure_examples.activity: Exploited CVE-2019-19781 (Citrix ADC), CVE-2019-11510 (Pulse Secure), CVE-2018-13379 (FortiGate), and CVE-2019-9670 (Zimbra) for initial access across multiple campaigns.
Exploited multiple Microsoft Exchange zero-day vulnerabilities (ProxyLogon) for both on-premises and edge-device compromise at scale.
Gained initial access to critical infrastructure targets through vulnerabilities in Fortinet, Ivanti, NETGEAR, Citrix, and Cisco appliances.
Exploited CVE-2018-0171 in Cisco's Smart Install feature to gain access to telecommunications infrastructure.
Exploited CVE-2021-44228 (Log4j) and ProxyShell variants as part of a broader espionage-focused initial-access campaign.
Exploited CVE-2018-13379 and CVE-2020-12812 (FortiOS) alongside CVE-2022-41040/41082 (Exchange ProxyNotShell) for initial access ahead of ransomware deployment.

data_sources.source: Web server / WAF logs (IIS, Apache, Nginx)
data_sources.detail: Abnormal HTTP methods, malformed requests, or a spike in 4xx/5xx error responses against a specific endpoint, especially correlated with the web service process subsequently spawning a shell.

w3wp.exe, httpd, nginx, or an equivalent web-facing service process spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, bash, or /bin/sh as a direct child process — one of the highest-confidence single signals in this entire pack.
Metadata service (169.254.169.254) access attempts from a workload process immediately following an ingress anomaly, or kubectl exec / sidecar spawn events correlated with abnormal ingress traffic.
SNMP or Smart Install anomalous input correlated with a CLI spawn or unexpected configuration change on the device.
OpenSLP service errors or restarts, or hostd/vpxd process anomalies correlated with unexpected datastore access changes.

detection_queries.title: Web Server Process Spawning Command Interpreter
detection_queries.description: Flags a web-facing service process (IIS, Apache, Nginx) directly spawning a shell or scripting engine, the highest-confidence single signature for successful exploitation of a public-facing application.
detection_queries.query:
title: Web Service Spawning Shell
id: 6a9d3c7e-8f4b-4c2a-9d1e-6a9d3c7e8f80
status: stable
author: H3AD-SEC Detection Engineering
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\w3wp.exe'
      - '\httpd.exe'
      - '\nginx.exe'
  selection_child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
  condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate web-application functionality that intentionally shells out to a helper script or utility as part of its designed behavior
level: critical
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190

detection_queries.title: Cloud Workload Metadata Service Access Following Ingress Anomaly
detection_queries.description: Correlates a spike in ALB/ELB error responses with subsequent metadata-service access from the same workload, consistent with a successful exploit pivoting toward cloud credential theft.
detection_queries.query:
AzureDiagnostics
| where Category == "ApplicationGatewayAccessLog" and httpStatus_d >= 400
| summarize ErrorCount = count() by bin(TimeGenerated, 5m), backendPoolName_s
| where ErrorCount > 20
| join kind=inner (
    AzureDiagnostics
    | where Category == "WorkloadMetadataAccess"
) on backendPoolName_s
| project TimeGenerated, backendPoolName_s, ErrorCount

false_positives: Legitimate web-application functionality that intentionally shells out to a local script or utility as part of its designed, documented behavior
Approved vulnerability scanning or penetration testing generating error-response spikes against the same application
Legitimate workload metadata access by an application that genuinely needs to retrieve its own instance credentials as part of normal operation
response_steps: Isolate the exploited application/host immediately and preserve web server logs, since they're frequently the only record of the initial exploit request itself
Identify the specific vulnerability or misconfiguration exploited and confirm whether a patch was available and how long it had been outstanding
Assume any credentials or tokens accessible to the exploited application's service account are compromised, especially in cloud/container environments where metadata-service access may have occurred
Check for lateral movement or ingress tool transfer originating from the compromised application host, since initial access via this technique is rarely the end objective on its own

mitigations.name: Update Software
mitigations.detail: Maintain rapid patch management specifically for internet-facing applications, with an accelerated response process for critical vulnerability disclosures rather than relying on routine patch cadence alone.

mitigations.name: Vulnerability Scanning
mitigations.detail: Regularly scan internet-facing systems and maintain an automated discovery process for newly-exposed services.

mitigations.name: Network Segmentation
mitigations.detail: Isolate public-facing servers in a DMZ, separate from internal infrastructure, to limit the blast radius of a successful exploit.

mitigations.name: Limit Access to Resource Over Network
mitigations.detail: Restrict public exposure to only the specific services genuinely intended for external use; move administrative interfaces off the public internet entirely.

mitigations.name: Filter Network Traffic
mitigations.detail: Deploy a Web Application Firewall to block known exploit patterns before they reach the application, and restrict outbound connections from public-facing servers to prevent post-exploit callback.

related.name: Ingress Tool Transfer
related.relation: The near-universal next step once a public-facing application is successfully exploited — pulling in the adversary's actual toolkit through the newly-obtained shell.

related.name: Container CLI/API
related.relation: Shares the containerized-environment variant of this technique, where exploitation of an ingress-exposed application leads directly into container/Kubernetes API abuse.

hypothesis.statement: A web-facing service process (w3wp.exe, httpd, nginx) spawns a command interpreter or scripting engine as a direct child process, or a cloud workload accesses its instance metadata service within minutes of an unusual spike in HTTP error responses.
hypothesis.rationale: Anchor detection on the shell-spawn behavior rather than any specific CVE signature -- the exploited vulnerability changes with every disclosure cycle, but a web service process becoming a shell's parent is a stable, durable signature that holds up regardless of which specific bug was used to get there.
